newsitem.title: UK: British Bankers' Association EMU report - summary.
newsitem.headline: British Bankers' Association EMU report - summary.

text.p: Following is the text of the summary and conclusions of the British Bankers' Association report "Preparing for EMU -- The implications of European Monetary Union for the banking and financial markets in the United Kingdom:"
SUMMARY AND CONCLUSIONS
General
4.1 The strength of political will in a number of Continental countries suggests that there is a strong probability that EMU will start in 1999 or soon afterwards.

4.2 The agreed transition to the single currency involves the single currency being used by the European Central Bank in money and foreign exchange markets from the outset and then spreading through the range of wholesale market activities and beyond. Euro cash would replace national notes and coin during the first six months of 2002.
4.3 Whether or not the UK participates in 1999, EMU will have significant implications for UK financial services markets, exchanges and individual institutions.
4.4 Notwithstanding the well documented strengths of UK financial markets and of the City of London in particular, to protect or enhance its position the City must:
- prepare for single currency functionality, with first
priority on efficient wholesale payments and settlement systems being in place by 1999 whether the UK participates or not.
- consider the options for retail banking systems,
which would need to be converted to the Euro if the UK decides to participate.
We note that the progress being made by APACS and the Clearing Companies is consistent with the necessary timescales.

4.5 The City needs to plan on the assumption that products, services, operations and supporting systems will need to accommodate use of the Euro in financial market activities and to support the needs of firms with international interests. Lead times for the required investments are such that decisions will be required in advance of certainty as to when EMU will start and which countries will participate. Though this involves a potential waste of resources, the alternative is the risk of severe competitive disadvantage to the City.
4.6 In the wholesale market, in particular, decisions on "rounding' and other market conventions, are required by the end of 1996.
Infrastructure

4.7 The appraisal of the changes to the trading, payment, processing, accounting and settlement systems required to accommodate the Euro should logically follow from a rigorous assessment of business needs, which should be put in hand without delay. Those changes also require a coordinated analysis of what is needed to ensure consistency with respect to timing, prospective transaction volumes and technical compatibility between the various elements of the infrastructure which support the UK's financial services.

4.8 If the UK does participate it will be necessary for the UK securities settlement systems (CMO, CGO and CREST) to be able to handle instruments denominated in the Euro; whether such facilities would be needed if the UK did not join the single currency remains under review.

4.9 The UK banking industry and individual institutions need to review the business, operational and systems implications of the options they face for effecting cross-border payments/settlement and obtaining access to Euro liquidity on the alternative assumptions of UK participation/non-participation. Those options include the ESCB TARGET system, Continental branch networks of UK banks, correspondent banking relationships, remote access and an enhanced ECU clearing system.

4.10 Competitive considerations argue for the development of high value Euro payment facilities in the UK. Attempts could be made to restrict the access of non-participating member states to TARGET on the grounds that it is a mechanism for facilitating monetary policy within the single monetary zone - although, as a payments system, it would be an integral part of the single market for financial services and as such should operate free from discrimination irrespective of whether a member state participates in EMU or not.

4.11 With regard to systems, a complicating factor is that the advent of the year 2000 will necessitate major computer adjustments during the same period the banking industry is preparing for EMU. Also, regulatory requirements and planned central utility updates can be anticipated to compete for systems resources. This combination of systems demands could amount to a considerable burden.
Financial Markets and Banking Sectors

4.12 General: A single currency denominated financial services market will, over time, intensify competition between the financial centres, markets, exchanges and individual institutions leading, in the long run, to restructuring and consolidation and the concentration of market share in the hands of fewer players. It is already clear that defensive domestic mergers, increased stake-holding, and cross-border acquisitions or alliances are under way or being contemplated in order to build positions in the future unified monetary zone. If successful, such developments would enable benefits of scale economies, cross-border relationships and delivery channels to be exploited (bearing in mind that for the foreseeable future, reputable local brands will not be displaced).
4.13 As to specific financial markets:
- money markets: if the UK were to participate, the

City would be a major centre for the Euro money and repo market (even though it would face the prospect of reserve requirements on Euro deposits which might involve a significant burden); non-participation may provide off-shore opportunities but the chance to become a major operational centre for the ESCB would be foregone; restrictions on access to TARGET/Euro liquidity could prove an impediment, though how significant this would be is not yet clear;
- bond markets: London's strength in secondary market

trading should remain, irrespective of UK participation; under a participation scenario, over the longer term opportunities for cross border primary dealing could emerge; with non-participation, UK firms could face greater competition for Euro issuance business of large corporates;
- equities: liquidity and the quality of

trading/settlement infrastructures rather than EMU will continue to be the main driver of competitive advantage and competition between European exchanges will increase as companies reduce the number of separate exchanges on which they need to be listed; under non participation, UK institutions would be less well placed to benefit if monetary union spurred greater issuance activity in the EMU area.
- foreign exchange markets: London is the dominant
global market; this position is unlikely to change in or out;
- derivatives: London is a major centre for both

exchange traded and OTC transactions; OTC business should continue to thrive irrespective of UK participation; for on exchange business, competition is likely to intensity but LIFFE should be well placed to meet the challenge;
- fund management: the industry does not expect EMU to
have a major effect on business, though the relaxation of currency matching constraints on EMU area institutional investors should create new opportunities;
- insurance: with regard to both life and general
business, the view of the industry appears to be that EMU is likely to have a fairly limited direct impact.

4.14 Decisions concerning the use of the Euro by the UK manufacturing and commercial sectors will have implications for the services to be provided by banks; industry needs to consider the extent to which and how quickly it would develop the use of the Euro, for example in funding or transactions with suppliers/customers (especially in Continental Europe) whether the UK participates or not. Although most UK firns have not yet addressed these issues in any detail, EMU would create demand for Euro-related banking services even if the UK were not to participate. Under a non participation scenario, UK institutions could face significant competition for the Euro business of large corporates from banks in the EMU area, particularly if they were less than thoroughly prepared for the single currency.

4.15 Extensive use of the Euro in personal/retail financial transactions if the UK were to participate would require substantial and costly changes to the supporting payments, accounting and settlement infrastructures:
- the elapsed times for such investments (3-4 years)

are such that if the UK were to participate in EMU in 1999 with a view to completing the changeover by 2002, detailed specification of the required investments would need to commence in 1997 in time for implementation from 1998;
- if a decision to participate were taken after early
1998 serious disruption would be created for UK financial services if a 2002 target date were retained;
- analyses of the existing capacity of the systems
within individual institutions and the inter-bank infrastructures to handle mass use of the Euro are priority tasks; work is already in hand by APACS.
Regulatory Environment

4.16 The possibility exists of discrimination against institutions/markets in non-participating member states. Whilst, in principle, such actions could be subject to legal challenge by the institutions affected, in practice this is not realistic.

4.17 It is to be hoped that the Commission will be vigilant in protecting single market freedoms and we propose possible new safeguarding provisions (see Section 2). In addition, a climate of good relations between the UK and other member states would be helpful in minimising problems in this area.

4.18 In the field of monetary policy, a decision has yet to be taken whether to use minimum reserve requirements. If the UK participated in EMU, the application of burdensome reserves could weaken the competitive position of UK (and other EMU area) banks. If the UK did not join the single currency, UK banks would have a relative advantage should minimum reserves be employed. The scale of any such advantage would depend on the parameters of the reserve system.

4.19 If the UK does participate, meeting the ECB data requirements will impose a significant additional reporting burden. A decision on participation will be taken in early 1998 and if the UK does decide to join the single currency this would leave banks with little time to make the necessary systems changes to provide requisite data.
Legal Certainty

4.20 It is essential that there should be certainty concerning the status of financial contracts denominated in national currencies which remain outstanding after the single currency has been introduced. A litigation risk exists that counterparties may seek to argue that the effect of EMU permits them to avoid their obligations, with consequential adverse implications for financial markets.

4.21 Therefore, legislation is needed to ensure that EMU should not be capable of being regarded as an excuse for breaking contracts unless the counterparties have agreed otherwise; the Commission proposal for a regulation is welcome but if (because of the UK opt-out) the UK does not fall within its scope, similar UK legislation is essential. It would be helpful for the UK government to make clear as soon as possible that in the event of the EU regulation not covering the UK, domestic regulation having the same effect would be progressed in good time for the start of 1999.
Conclusions

4.22 The economic effects of the single currency and the implications for financial markets cannot be predicted with any certainty, whether or not the UK participates. Despite the considerable strengths of London as a global financial centre, there can be no room for complacency. Much is likely to depend on UK markets making necessary preparations in a timely manner.

4.23 We welcome the steps the Bank of England has taken since the transition scenario was settled at the end of last year to encourage coordination in preparations for EMU and acknowledge the valuable work being undertaken by the Bank itself. In view of the importance of being in a state of readiness for EMU, we believe that a mapping exercise detailing necessary preparations across the financial markets as a whole would be a worthwhile complementary measure.

4.24 Participation in EMU would have such major implications for the financial sector and for the entire economy that only the government itself could provide the necessary leadership and coordination.
4.25 Despite the considerable uncertainties, we believe:
- London would be strongly placed to attract Euro
business across a broad range of markets if the UK participates in monetary union.
- In the event of non-participation, UK markets would

still attract considerable Euro business. If the EMU area were to be characterised by a high regulation culture, the competitive position of the City would be strengthened further. At the same time, the advent of a single currency should lead to greater economic integration in the EMU area and, should monetary union prove to be an economic success, London would probably be less favourably positioned to take advantage of the considerable business opportunities that would be likely to ensue.
- While an offshore scenario would offer certain

advantages, the UK could face discrimination from participating member states and any serious perception of a UK "sidelined' in the EU may discourage institutions from basing new operations in the UK. If the UK does not join the single currency, it would be important for the UK to maintain a constructive relationship with participating member states.
- Overall, provided that thorough preparations are put
in hand, the UK financial sector should continue to prosper regardless of participation in monetary union.
-- Richard Murphy, London Newsroom +44 171 542 2774
